In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the form of the book is not just a formalist concern, but rather that it is the form of the decolonial struggle itself.

Derrida's engagement with Genet in Glas, and the form he creates for it, is not just another instance of his “deconstruction of philosophy” but also a decolonial engagement with the forms of knowledge, and writing, that have been at the heart of the European colonial enterprise.
Derrida and his writing are not only the “last Jews” (as he has been often called) but also the first Palestinians.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Derrida and Glas, in their engagement with the Palestinian struggle, offer a new way of thinking the political, a new form for decolonial politics.

the textuality and form of Glas are a political intervention in the history of philosophy, a deconstruction of the dialectic of the Same and the Other, a critique of European coloniality, and the invention of a new form for anti-colonization.
Derrida's reading of Genet, and his own writing, is a decolonial reading of the dialectic, a reading that is both a reading of the Jew and a reading of the Palestinian.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Derrida’s deconstruction is not only a critique of the philosophical tradition but also a critique of the form of the philosophical tradition, and that the latter is in fact a decolonial project.

Derrida’s Glas, and the book’s decolonial form, can be read as a response to the political situation of the Palestinian liberation struggle and the anti-colonial struggle of the Third World more broadly.
, as Derrida’s reading of Genet’s political writings shows, deconstruction is not only an intellectual practice but also an ethical-political imperative.
